newsitem.title: USA: Warnaco completes sale of Hathaway division.
newsitem.headline: Warnaco completes sale of Hathaway division.

text.p: Warnaco Group Inc has completed the sale of C.F. Hathaway Co. to an investment group that includes former Gov. John McKernan and former Capital Cities/ABC president Daniel Burke, officials said Wednesday.

Warnaco, which received international criticism when announced plans to sell or close the 159-year-old maker of men's shirts, retains an option to purchase a 20 percent stake in the new company in three years.

The price of the sale was not disclosed. The deal includes the Hathaway brand name and the company's 450-employee factory in Waterville and 169-employee facility in Prescott, Ontario., officials said.

"The company's heritage and the fact that Hathaway's workers traditionally have been known as the finest shirtmakers in the world led to a great deal of interest in the company by a great number of people," McKernan said in a prepared statement.

Hathaway is the oldest shirtmaking company in the United States. The company is best known for its long-running "Man in the Hathaway shirt" advertising campaign that featured celebrities and well-known businessmen wearing black eye patches.

Warnaco announced in May that it would dispose of Hathaway because of declining sales. The move was attacked because it came as Warnaco was earning record profits and after Hathaway's employees had sharply increased productivity.

"We are very pleased to complete a transaction that serves the stategic needs of the company and its shareholders, as well as preserves the jobs of workers at Hathaway," Warnaco CEO Linda Wachner said.
The investment group has received concessions from Hathaway's workers, and $1.6 million tax incentives and grant aid from state, local and federal governments.
The advertising giant, McCann-Erickson will represent the new company, which had sales of $43 million in 1995.

In addition to McKernan and Burke the investors include British Aerospace chairman Robert Bauman, Maine businessman Michael Liberty and three Pennsylvania-based investment groups; Keystone Venture IV, G-II Family Partnership and Glenville Capital Partners.
